nameStory: The word 'vetch' comes from the Latin 'vicia,' which ancient Romans used for these climbing legumes. Common vetch earned its straightforward name by being the most widespread and familiar member of the vetch family worldwide. Sometimes called 'tare,' an old English word meaning 'weed,' it reflects this plant's tendency to pop up uninvited in grain fields.
description: Common vetch is a climbing annual plant that scrambles up through grasses and other vegetation using delicate tendrils. It typically grows 1-3 feet tall, with compound leaves made up of small oval leaflets arranged in pairs along the stem. The purple-pink pea-like flowers appear singly or in pairs, followed by flattened brown seed pods. This nitrogen-fixing legume spreads readily and can form dense patches in disturbed soils.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Purple-pink pea-shaped flowers about half an inch long, appearing alone or in pairs directly from the leaf joints. The flowers have the classic legume structure with an upper banner petal and lower keel, and feel slightly papery when touched.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 8-16 oval leaflets arranged in pairs, ending in branched curly tendrils that feel wiry and grip tightly to whatever they touch. The leaflets are smooth and soft, about half an inch long.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Climbing or sprawling vine-like plant that uses its tendrils to scramble through other vegetation. Stems are weak and need support, feeling smooth and slightly angular when rolled between your fingers.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Flattened brown pods about 1-2 inches long that feel papery and rattle when shaken. The pods split open to reveal 4-8 round brown seeds that are smooth and hard to the touch.

habitat: Common vetch thrives in disturbed soils including roadsides, field edges, waste areas, and abandoned lots throughout New England. It prefers full sun to partial shade and tolerates poor, dry soils better than most legumes. You'll often find it climbing through grasses in old fields or growing along fence rows and pathway edges.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge with their distinctive compound leaves and begin sending out tendrils to climb nearby vegetation. Early spring growth is bright green and tender.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs with purple-pink flowers appearing throughout the season. Plants reach full size and begin producing their characteristic flattened seed pods.
seasonality.fall: Seed pods ripen to brown and split open, releasing seeds. The annual plants begin to yellow and die back as temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Plants are completely dead and gone, leaving only seeds in the soil to germinate the following spring.

funFact: Common vetch is nature's fertilizer factory - bacteria in its root nodules can capture nitrogen from the air and convert it into plant food, which is why farmers sometimes grow it specifically to enrich poor soils even though the seeds contain compounds that make them unsuitable for human consumption.
confusionNotes: Common vetch can be confused with other climbing vetches, but most have flowers in clusters rather than single or paired flowers. Wild pea has similar flowers but larger, more triangular leaflets and lacks the distinctive branched tendrils.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'common' and looking harmless, the seeds contain compounds that can be toxic to humans and some livestock if eaten in large quantities. However, the plant itself has been used as animal fodder and green manure for centuries.
compareHints: Common vetch stands out from its relatives by having flowers that appear singly or in pairs rather than in clusters like tufted vetch or hairy vetch. Its leaflets are broader and more oval than the narrow leaflets of hairy vetch, and it lacks the dense fuzzy coating that gives hairy vetch its name. The branched tendrils and purple-pink flowers distinguish it from yellow-flowered large yellow vetch.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Tufted vetch stands out from its vetch relatives by having the most densely packed, one-sided flower clusters that hang downward like purple bunches of grapes.

Among the vetches in New England, hairy vetch stands out for its distinctly fuzzy stems - tufted vetch has smooth stems, common vetch has larger individual flowers, and the smaller vetches like hairy tare have much tinier flowers and leaflets.
Among New England vetches, lentil vetch is the smallest and most delicate, with the tiniest flowers and smoothest texture.

Among New England's vetches, bush vetch stands out for its short flower clusters of just 2-6 blooms, while tufted vetch has long, showy spikes of many flowers and hairy vetch has dense, cone-shaped clusters.
Hairy tare stands out from its vetch relatives primarily by size - everything about it is smaller and more delicate.
Among the vetch family in New England, large yellow vetch is unmistakable due to its bright yellow flowers - all other local vetches have purple, pink, or white blooms.
Among New England's vetches, spring vetch stands out for its diminutive size - both the flowers and overall plant are much smaller than tufted vetch or hairy vetch.
Unlike other vetches in New England, fava beans are much larger, bushier plants that don't climb or sprawl.
